result:
The world is loud, but mornings still hold their quiet magic. I love the way light slides across a wooden floor like spilled honey, slow and golden, catching dust motes in lazy spirals. There’s something sacred about that first cup of coffee, steam rising like incense, while the city outside hasn’t yet remembered how to be cruel.

I’ve been thinking lately about how everything worth keeping is fragile. A handwritten letter, the particular laugh of someone you love, the way certain songs feel like they were written only for the version of you that existed at sixteen. We spend so much time building armor when perhaps we should be practicing tenderness instead.

Yesterday I watched an old man feed pigeons in the park with the solemn devotion of a monk. Each crumb was offered with care, as if he understood that small generosities are the only currency that matters. The birds didn’t thank him with words, but they stayed. That felt like enough.

I want to live more like that: deliberate, soft, paying attention. Collecting moments instead of things. Learning the names of neighborhood trees. Remembering that every stranger on the train is carrying an entire universe inside their chest, just like I am.

The older I get, the more convinced I become that the revolution we need isn’t loud or violent. It’s quieter. It looks like choosing patience when anger would be easier. Choosing to repair instead of discard. Choosing to see.

And maybe, just maybe, choosing to write 250 words about nothing in particular, simply because the light is beautiful this morning and someone, somewhere, might need to remember that beauty still exists. (248)
